evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 19: tēlum ē corpore (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The general word: a weapon from a wound, a net from the water, a person from hiding. Pliny uses dentēs extrahere of drawing teeth with remedies, dentem ēvellere of pulling one by force (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: pull out, tear out (teeth, nails, weeds)
terms.comment: To pull out by force; figuratively to root out (a worry, a memory): a favourite of Cicero’s (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Plin. NH 20.3: sūcum expressō sēminī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: For extracting a juice or an oil (see squeeze-out). An extract in the chemist’s sense is extractum (M-O s.v. preparation: extract; nineteenth-century pharmacy).

phrases.latin: quasi pōma ex arboribus, crūda sī sunt, vix ēvelluntur, sī mātūra et cocta, dēcidunt
phrases.english: like apples on trees: if they are unripe, they can hardly be pulled off; if ripe and mellow, they fall

phrases.latin: delphīnum gestātōrem collūsōremque puerōrum in terram quoque extrahī solitum
phrases.english: the dolphin, the boys’ carrier and playmate, used to be pulled up onto the shore too

sources: Lewis & Short: extraho · Lewis & Short: evello · Lewis & Short: exprimo
Cicero and Pliny from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica, loci-plinius); the other passages as Lewis & Short quotes them.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. preparation: extract.
